capstone: Build a small but realistic payroll-and-projects database in SQLite from scratch: design a normalized schema (departments, employees, projects, assignments), populate it with 30+ rows of your own invented data, create indexes on foreign keys and common search columns, then answer five reporting questions with queries that use a join, a CTE, a window function, a set operation, and a transaction-safe update. Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on each and confirm the index usage.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Given an existing table customers with a UNIQUE email column, which single statement raises its balance column by 100 for every row where balance is negative?
Explain the difference between TRUNCATE TABLE (where supported) and DELETE FROM with no WHERE clause, in terms of what is logged and what can be rolled back.
Describe, in your own words, what happens if an UPDATE statement matches zero rows.
Write the SQLite pragma that lists the columns of a table, and state what a T-SQL equivalent would be (hint: information_schema or sp_help).
keyConcepts: Schemas, databases, and tables: organizing containers for rows
Column data types and why SQLite type affinity matters
Primary keys, foreign keys, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT constraints
CREATE/ALTER/DROP TABLE as schema-change tools
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE as row-change tools
The full read-modify cycle: SELECT it, UPDATE it, DELETE it, re-verify
labs: Lab 1.1 — Create company.db and build a departments table: CREATE TABLE departments (dept_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, budget INTEGER CHECK (budget >= 0)). Insert 4 departments. Dialect note: SQLite's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY auto-increments without the AUTOINCREMENT keyword; SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1), Oracle uses sequences. AUTOINCREMENT in SQLite is optional and adds a bookkeeping table.

Lab 1.2 — Build employees (emp_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, dept_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(dept_id), salary INTEGER, hire_date TEXT). Insert 8 employees, two per department. Dialect note: store dates as TEXT in ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' form in SQLite; SQL Server has a real DATE type and Oracle uses DATE; comparisons on ISO text sort correctly.

Lab 1.3 — Practice DML: give every employee in one department a 5% raise (UPDATE with WHERE), fix a misspelled name, delete one employee row, then re-run SELECT COUNT(*) to verify. Wrap the three changes in BEGIN; ... COMMIT; and re-run with ROLLBACK first to see changes vanish.

Lab 1.4 — Alter the schema without losing data: ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN email TEXT UNIQUE; update rows to fill it in. Dialect note: SQLite ALTER TABLE cannot drop a column (historically) or modify a type — the standard workaround is CREATE new table, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, DROP old, RENAME. SQL Server supports ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN directly.

Lab 1.5 — Explore the schema: run .schema employees and PRAGMA table_info(employees); in the sqlite3 CLI. Note what sqlite3 prints for the primary key and foreign key, and which of those it enforces by default.
objectives: Create, alter, and drop tables using standard DDL with constraints
Insert, update, and delete rows safely with WHERE clauses and transactions
Describe how SQLite's type affinity differs from strict-typed engines
Recover from a schema-migration mistake using the rebuild pattern
modules.title: Module 1 — DDL and DML Fundamentals

checkpoints: Predict the result of WHERE salary = NULL versus WHERE salary IS NULL — and explain why.
Rewrite a HAVING clause as a WHERE clause in a query where it is valid to do so, and state where the rewrite breaks.
Given daily sales rows, which clause filters individual sales above 1000 and which filters stores whose total sales are below 10000?
Write the logical execution order of SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT from memory.
keyConcepts: SELECT column list, DISTINCT, and column aliases
WHERE predicates: comparisons, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL
Logical evaluation order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and NULL handling
GROUP BY buckets and HAVING post-aggregation filters
ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET for paging
labs: Lab 2.1 — Seed an orders table (order_id, customer, amount, region, order_date). Write queries: all orders from 'West' over 500; customers whose names start with 'A' (LIKE 'A%'); all rows where shipped is NULL vs IS NULL. Observe that NULL never equals anything.

Lab 2.2 — Aggregation: compute COUNT(*), COUNT(customer), SUM(amount), AVG(amount), MIN/MAX(amount) over orders. Run COUNT(customer) after inserting a row with NULL customer and note the difference from COUNT(*) — aggregates ignore NULLs except COUNT(*).

Lab 2.3 — Group and filter groups: SELECT region, COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 5000. Then try moving the SUM condition into WHERE and record the error — WHERE cannot see aggregates because it runs before grouping.

Lab 2.4 — Paging drill: ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5 returns rows 6–10 by amount. Dialect note: SQL Server uses SELECT TOP 5 ... (no OFFSET equivalent without ORDER BY + OFFSET/FETCH), Oracle 12c+ uses FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY (older Oracle: WHERE ROWNUM <= 5). LIMIT is SQLite/Postgres/MySQL.

Lab 2.5 — String/date practice: concatenate first and last name with || (SQLite/Postgres/Oracle; SQL Server uses +). Extract the order year with strftime('%Y', order_date) — dialect note: SQL Server uses YEAR() or DATEPART, Postgres EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ...).
objectives: Filter rows precisely with WHERE predicates including NULL semantics
Aggregate with GROUP BY and separate row filters from group filters (WHERE vs HAVING)
Page and sort result sets portably across dialects
Translate basic date/string functions between SQLite and T-SQL
modules.title: Module 2 — Filtering and Aggregation

checkpoints: Draw the Venn-diagram overlap for INNER vs LEFT JOIN on employees ⋈ departments and state which side keeps its unmatched rows.
A self-join query returns each pair twice (A-B and B-A). What single predicate removes the duplicates?
State the row-count formula for a CROSS JOIN and explain when you would actually want one.
Explain what happens to columns when a FULL OUTER JOIN is simulated in SQLite with a UNION of LEFT and RIGHT joins.
keyConcepts: INNER JOIN: matching rows only, the default workhorse
LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN: preserving unmatched rows from one or both sides
Table aliases and why join queries need them
Self-joins: a table joined to itself for hierarchies
CROSS JOIN: the cartesian product and its row-count math
Multi-table join chains and join-order readability
labs: Lab 3.1 — INNER JOIN employees to departments on dept_id; select employee name, department name, salary. Then change INNER to LEFT JOIN and add an employee with a NULL dept_id — observe the new row with a NULL department name. Dialect note: join syntax is identical across SQLite, SQL Server, Postgres, Oracle.

Lab 3.2 — Self-join hierarchy: ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(emp_id). Set managers, then SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id. LEFT JOIN keeps the CEO (no manager).

Lab 3.3 — CROSS JOIN experiment: SELECT d.dept_name, p.proj_name FROM departments d CROSS JOIN (small projects table) — count the rows and verify it equals departments × projects. Then rewrite the same query with a comma-style join and an explicit ON 1=1 to see the equivalence.

Lab 3.4 — FULL OUTER JOIN in SQLite: SQLite has no FULL OUTER JOIN keyword (Postgres and SQL Server do). Simulate it: LEFT JOIN query UNION RIGHT-equivalent (swap table order) LEFT JOIN. Compare the result to the INNER JOIN row count and account for every extra row.
objectives: Write inner and outer joins with correct ON conditions and aliases
Model a hierarchy with a self-join and keep the root rows
Predict and verify cross-join row counts
Simulate FULL OUTER JOIN in SQLite with UNION
modules.title: Module 3 — Joins: Inner, Outer, Self, Cross

checkpoints: Convert a correlated subquery to an equivalent JOIN and state which reads more clearly for 'employees earning above their department average'.
Explain why a scalar subquery must return at most one row, and what error you get otherwise.
Rewrite a three-level nested subquery as a chain of two CTEs and compare readability.
State one thing a recursive CTE can do that a plain subquery cannot.
keyConcepts: Scalar, row, and table subqueries in SELECT, WHERE, and FROM
Correlated vs uncorrelated subqueries and how the engine evaluates them
EXISTS vs IN: semantics and NULL pitfalls
Common Table Expressions (WITH) for readability and reuse
Chained CTEs: building a query in named steps
Recursive CTEs: traversing hierarchies and sequences
labs: Lab 4.1 — Scalar subquery: SELECT name, salary, (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS avg_sal FROM employees — one value broadcast per row. Then correlate it: employees earning more than the average of THEIR department, with the inner query referencing the outer alias.

Lab 4.2 — EXISTS vs IN: find departments with no employees using NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id). Insert a NULL dept_id employee and show that NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees) silently returns nothing — the classic NULL trap; NOT EXISTS is immune.

Lab 4.3 — CTE readability: rewrite Lab 4.1's correlated query as WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) a FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN dept_avg d ON ... WHERE e.salary > d.a. Chain a second CTE that ranks the result.

Lab 4.4 — Recursive CTE: WITH RECURSIVE reports(emp_id, name, lvl) AS (SELECT emp_id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, r.lvl+1 FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.emp_id) SELECT * FROM reports. Print the org chart with indentation via lvl.
objectives: Choose between scalar, correlated, and EXISTS subqueries for a task
Avoid the NOT IN / NULL trap with NOT EXISTS
Refactor nested subqueries into readable chained CTEs
Traverse a hierarchy with a recursive CTE
modules.title: Module 4 — Subqueries and CTEs

checkpoints: State the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK on tied values.
Explain what happens to a window function's result when the PARTITION BY is removed.
Predict the output of SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) on five rows.
Name two reporting questions that are painful without window functions but trivial with them.
keyConcepts: OVER() clause: computing across rows without collapsing them
PARTITION BY: independent calculations per group
ORDER BY inside OVER and frame boundaries
Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
Running totals and moving averages with ROWS frames
LAG/LEAD: reaching into neighboring rows
labs: Lab 5.1 — Ranking per department: SELECT name, dept_id, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rn, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) r, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) dr FROM employees. Insert two employees with identical salaries and compare the three columns on the tie.

Lab 5.2 — Running totals: monthly sales table; SELECT month, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running FROM sales. Then change the frame to ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 3-month moving total. Dialect note: window functions are standard SQL and work identically in SQLite (3.25+), Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle.

Lab 5.3 — LAG/LEAD deltas: SELECT month, amount, amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS mom_change FROM sales. Handle the first row's NULL with COALESCE(..., 0). Note FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE exist too — try FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY month).

Lab 5.4 — Top-N per group, the window way: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM employees) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 2. Compare with the GROUP BY approach from Module 2 and note what information GROUP BY loses (the actual rows).
objectives: Compute rankings, running totals, and moving aggregates without collapsing rows
Choose correctly between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK
Use LAG/LEAD and frames for period-over-period analysis
Solve top-N-per-group problems with window functions
modules.title: Module 5 — Window Functions

checkpoints: State the column-count and type-compatibility rules that UNION enforces.
Explain the practical difference between UNION and UNION ALL on a 10-million-row append.
Show how INTERSECT answers 'customers who bought in BOTH January and February'.
Describe what EXCEPT returns that a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right IS NULL does not make obvious.
keyConcepts: UNION vs UNION ALL: deduplicated vs raw appends
Column alignment rules across set-operation branches
INTERSECT: rows present in both sets
EXCEPT: rows in the first set but not the second
Set operations as an alternative to joins for membership questions
Dialect note: Oracle calls EXCEPT 'MINUS'
labs: Lab 6.1 — UNION ALL drill: two regional sales tables with identical schemas; SELECT region, amount FROM sales_east UNION ALL SELECT region, amount FROM sales_west. Count rows, then switch to UNION and count again — the duplicate rows disappear. Explain which is cheaper and why (no sort/dedupe pass).

Lab 6.2 — Type-alignment trap: attempt a UNION between a TEXT column and an INTEGER column and observe SQLite's lenient coercion; note that SQL Server would raise a conversion error. Fix the query with CAST(amount AS TEXT). Dialect note: always CAST explicitly for portable set queries.

Lab 6.3 — INTERSECT: customers who ordered in both Q1 and Q2: SELECT customer FROM orders WHERE quarter='Q1' INTERSECT SELECT customer FROM orders WHERE quarter='Q2'. Rewrite with an INNER JOIN of two DISTINCT subqueries and compare plans with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
Lab 6.4 — EXCEPT and the Oracle name: employees in Engineering EXCEPT employees assigned to Project X. Dialect note: Oracle spells this operator MINUS; Postgres, SQL Server, and SQLite use EXCEPT.
objectives: Combine result sets with UNION/UNION ALL and explain the cost difference
Answer membership questions with INTERSECT and EXCEPT
Enforce column alignment with explicit CASTs for portability
Translate EXCEPT to Oracle's MINUS
modules.title: Module 6 — Set Operations

checkpoints: List the four ACID properties and give a one-sentence failure scenario each prevents.
Explain the difference between BEGIN DEFERRED and BEGIN IMMEDIATE in SQLite locking terms.
Describe a dirty read in plain language and name the isolation level that permits it.
State what happens to an uncommitted transaction when the sqlite3 CLI exits.
keyConcepts: ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK and savepoints
SQLite locking: DEFERRED, IMMEDIATE, EXCLUSIVE
The four standard isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED → SERIALIZABLE
Dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads
Lost updates and why read-modify-write needs a transaction
labs: Lab 7.1 — Atomic transfer: two account rows; BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT; Verify totals unchanged. Then repeat but run ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT after the first UPDATE — show the balances revert. Open two sqlite3 sessions to try overlapping writes and observe the second session's 'database is locked' behavior.

Lab 7.2 — Savepoints: BEGIN; UPDATE ...; SAVEPOINT sp1; UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK TO sp1; COMMIT; Show that only the pre-savepoint change survived. Note savepoints are standard SQL and work the same in Postgres and SQL Server (SAVE TRANSACTION in T-SQL).

Lab 7.3 — Lost-update demo: read a counter value in two sessions, have both add 1 and write back — the counter only goes up by 1. Fix it by wrapping read+write in BEGIN IMMEDIATE; ... COMMIT; so the second session waits. Dialect note: Postgres/SQL Server solve the same problem with row locks or SERIALIZABLE; SQLite's coarse locking makes BEGIN IMMEDIATE the tool.

Lab 7.4 — Isolation vocabulary: read the SQLite transaction docs and write a one-paragraph summary of why SQLite documents no SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL — its locking gives SERIALIZABLE behavior by default. Dialect note: SQL Server defaults to READ COMMITTED; Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED too. Contrast with SQLite in your notes.
objectives: Wrap multi-statement changes in atomic transactions with savepoints
Demonstrate and fix a lost update with proper locking
Explain the four isolation levels and the anomalies each prevents
Contrast SQLite's locking model with SQL Server/Postgres isolation settings
modules.title: Module 7 — Transactions and Isolation

checkpoints: State the two questions an index answers faster, and the two costs every index charges.
Read an EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN line and identify SCAN vs SEARCH and which index was used.
Explain why indexing every column is worse than indexing none on a write-heavy table.
Give a real example of a query that got slower after denormalization, or explain why that can happen.
keyConcepts: B-tree indexes: ordered lookups, range scans, sorting
When indexes help: selective WHERE, JOIN keys, ORDER BY
When indexes hurt: write amplification and storage
Reading EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: SCAN vs SEARCH, covering indexes
Composite indexes and leftmost-prefix rule
Normalization forms 1NF–3NF vs deliberate denormalization trade-offs
labs: Lab 8.1 — Measure before/after: create orders_big with 100,000 rows (generate with a recursive CTE INSERT). Time SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders_big WHERE customer='C042' with .timer on. CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders_big(customer); re-time and record the speedup. Then run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the query and point to the SEARCH line naming your index.

Lab 8.2 — Composite index: query WHERE region='West' AND amount > 1000 ORDER BY order_date. Create (region, amount) and compare plans against separate single-column indexes. Try swapping the column order and explain which prefix the WHERE clause can use — the leftmost-prefix rule in action.

Lab 8.3 — Write cost: time inserting 10,000 rows into a table with 5 indexes vs the same table with none (DROP INDEX, re-time). Record the slowdown percentage — this is write amplification, the reason for index discipline.

Lab 8.4 — Normalize then denormalize on purpose: start with a flat sales_flat table (repeating customer name/address per row), normalize to customers + sales (1NF: atomic values, 2NF/3NF: no partial or transitive dependencies — address depends on customer, not on the sale). Then add a denormalized total_spent column to customers maintained by a trigger, and argue in writing when each shape wins. Dialect note: CREATE INDEX and EXPLAIN syntax is near-identical across SQLite, Postgres, and SQL Server (SQL Server: SET SHOWPLAN or graphical plans).
objectives: Create and evaluate indexes with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
Apply the composite-index leftmost-prefix rule
Quantify the write cost of over-indexing
Normalize to 3NF and justify deliberate denormalization
modules.title: Module 8 — Indexes, Query Plans, and Normalization

objectives: Design and evolve a relational schema using DDL with constraints
Write correct multi-table queries using joins, subqueries, CTEs, and window functions
